newsitem.title: USA: State Dept denies harrasing activist.
newsitem.headline: State Dept denies harrasing activist.

text.p: The State Department denied on Tuesday that it was harrassing a Kurdish activist charged with grand theft and forgery in connection with student loans obtained in the name of a dead child.
"And the charge that somehow the State Department is harassing this guy -- it's just baseless," spokesman Nicholas Burns told reporters.
"Now, these charges are very serious -- nine counts of felony. They were brought by the district attorney in Santa Barbara. They are not State Department charges," he said.
Activist Kani Xulam, convicted in 1996 of passport fraud, was arrested for a second time last Friday by Washington D.C. police and State Department diplomatic security agents.
He was charged with grand theft, perjury and forgery for fraudulently obtaining more than $13,000 in federal and state college aid, authorities said.

In a telephone interview with Reuters on Monday, Xulam said: "I have cooperated with the authorities in every instance and find the continuous harassment by the United States State Department unjustified."

Turkish officials have accused Xulam of being a leader of the Kurdistan Worker's Party (PKK), which is fighting for independence or autonomy from Turkey, a close NATO ally. The United States considers the PKK a terrorist group.

Xulam, who was freed on his own recognisance, insisted neither he nor his American Kurdish Information Network are affiliated with terrorist groups. "AKIN is a non-profit human rights organisation promoting the human rights of the Kurds," he said, adding he fled Turkey years ago "because there was repression there."
Xulam headed AKIN when first arrested in April 1996 and charged with passport fraud after a State Department probe.

He was convicted in the first case of obtaining and using a passport in the name of Steven Barry Citron, an 18-month-old boy who was killed with his family in a car crash in Louisiana in 1993. Xulam assumed his identity. His sentence was three years probation and 400 hours of community service.

Friday's arrest was based on charges brought by Santa Barbara County, California, which alleged he obtained a total of $13,257 in student grants and loans provided by the federal and state governments when he attended Santa Barbara City College and the University of California at Santa Barbara.
Xulam used Citron's name to enroll in the colleges, obtain the loans, sign the checks and get a driver's license, according to the arrest warrant.
